I didn't know him from before and I didn't know what his position in the army was. In other words, I met Mr. Jankovic, or Colonel Jankovic, then and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did Momir Nikolic tell you anything about what unit in the VRS he belonged to; whether he belonged to a superior unit, a subordinate unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No. He didn't say anything other than to report to him, and he pointed him out, he actually pointed to the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As you sit here today, can you tell us, do you know what position Colonel Jankovic had back in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what his position was in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you were assigned this task by Colonel Jankovic, did he tell you in particular what to do, that is, how to go about counting this massive number of people that you saw in Potocari when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He did not explain the manner in how I should do that but he just wanted me to report what the number of persons on buses and trucks was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And how did you go about doing that? If you could tell us just briefly how you did it.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The first two to three hours after I received this assignment, a few colleagues, military policemen and I, literally counted every single person boarding a vehicle. We stood, usually two of us, at the door and we would count the persons getting on. However, if we did not succeed in doing that, if a larger number of people came in at the same time, we would sometimes even go on the bus and count them over, but normally we would just count every single individual boarding the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: After these first two or three hours, how did you count the number of individuals that were being bussed out of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: After the first two to three hours, I proposed to Colonel Jankovic -- and it was my own proposal, I asked for his approval, because it was impossible to count all the people in this manner, and the crowds were getting bigger and bigger, so I proposed that we just count, as a sample, the number of people on a bus or a truck, and those figures would usually be approximately similar. In other words, a similar number of people would fit in a bus or a truck. So I asked him if we could just count the number of buses and then later on to reconstruct and come to an approximate figure of the total number of people. And he approved of that method.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How many people did you estimate -- I think I read in your transcript, and you can correct me if you're [sic] wrong but you estimated about 70 people for a bus; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. My answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how many people did you estimate could fit in a truck?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Large trucks were used mainly for women and children. These were huge trucks that could fit 150 to 170 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you approached Colonel Jankovic about this method that you were going to use, and he approved that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in your testimony you mentioned someone by the name of Milisav Ilic. Do you remember that? I think you mentioned that he was a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Milisav Ilic was a police officer. I mentioned him because he was on a similar assignment in those couple of days as I was. In other words, determining the exact -- establishing the exact number of persons leaving that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you work with him in order to work out the number of individuals that you were counting, that were being bussed out of Potocari, or did you work independently of him, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We worked independently. I've already said that. He did not go on or into any of the buses. I know that he asked me to tell him what the approximate number of individuals that could fit in a bus or a truck would be. We did have a brief meeting with Colonel Jankovic on the next day, because he told us that we should be more careful about figuring out the number of persons who were leaving the area, and I concluded, based on that, that he had information both that I provided on the number of individuals as well as information provided by Milisav Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of the information that you provided Colonel Jankovic, did you provide that to him periodically or was that an end-of-day tally or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: At the end of the day certainly there was a total tally, as it were, and -- but we also had contacts, several contacts during the day so that I would keep him up to date on the number of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the contacts that you had with him periodically during the day, was that just with you and Colonel Jankovic, or were there other individuals also involved during these contacts?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: On several occasions I approached him briefly, but there was also an occasion on the following day when Mr. Milisav Ilic was present too, and that's when he actually told us to be more careful about the figures we were providing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you the only member of the military police from your brigade that was participating in counting the individuals in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: On the first day, in those first two to three hours, I had help from a number of colleagues, a couple of colleagues. Later on, when we started counting the vehicles and then give a breakdown of the individuals per vehicle, at the end, I could do the job myself, there was no need for anyone else to be there, and then the final figure could be deduced from that at the end. It didn't have to be done immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The colleagues that you're referring to, were they members of the military police as well?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were colleagues of mine, military police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you remember their names, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can name a few names for sure: Radenko Zaric, Milovan Mitrovic, Milan Gvozdenovic. Those would be the names I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you in uniform, if you recall, during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you just describe your uniform so the Trial Chamber has a clear picture of what it looked like?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We had uniform uniforms, as it were. They were green camouflage uniforms. The whole brigade wore the same kind of uniform. We didn't -- the military police did not have a special uniform, but we did have white belts, and that stood out, and we also had emblems on our left sleeve. We also wore ribbons. They were some 10 to 12 centimetres long. We would put them on our left sleeve, and you could make us out easily. And there was also the words of the brigade, you know, so it was really quite visible, it stood out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about the separated men. In your testimony, and once again you correct me if I'm wrong, but in your testimony you indicated that you saw men being separated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where was this? When and where was it?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The men were separated before they reached the vehicle. They were separated on the way from when they left the line where there was this red and white ribbon, then they would let through a group of people, men, women and children, and as they were going towards us, they would go through two lines of police, special military police, the men were separated, and the group that was going towards Srebrenica was on the right-hand side, and the buses were on the right-hand side, if you look from Bratunac to Srebrenica, so the men were separated there, and the women and children would board the buses which were on the right-hand side of the road from Srebrenica to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: After the men were separated, or during the separation process, can you tell us, were you able to see where they were taken or where they went?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I could see, because they went by me and towards the bus, and I was always around the buses. They would pass by the bus along the left side of the bus, they would continue on, and then they would take a turn to the left, towards a white house, on the left side of the road from Srebrenica to Bratunac. They would remain there, and once the yard was full of people, because that's what was done on the first day, they would be brought to the yard of that building, of that house, and they would be kept there, but later on, there were too many people so they would just remain on the side of the road, in the meadows, they would sit there and wait for the transport to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you able to see if there were -- there was a military presence near that white house where you saw these separated men being taken? Did you recognise anybody there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that this line through which they had to, or by which they had to pass was numerous, there were many of them present there, and I'm talking about the line of soldiers that was there by which the people would have to go to that -- to get to the house, but how many of them there were, I don't know, I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you yourself have any occasion to go by that house?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't go by that house because there was no need for that. The house was opposite the area where I remained those two days, but I could see the house from there and I could see the yard as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you see Colonel Jankovic go by that house while you were there or in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The house was on the left-hand side of the road going from -- to Bratunac from Srebrenica. Colonel Jankovic was not frequently on the side where I was, and I was on the opposite side. He was usually on the opposite side. And he spent most of his time with his back turned to the yard of that house. Some ten metres perhaps was the yard of that house, some ten metres behind his back. But on one occasion, and I was present there, he actually addressed the people who were in the yard but I never saw him going into the yard or into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When he addressed the people in the yard, did you happen to hear what he said? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Tell us what he said and let us know what people you're talking about that he addressed.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: What he said happened after a mutiny of sorts, if I can call it that. Well, there was a commotion in that crowd of people, in the yard. I heard them beginning to ask, "Why are we being separated from the women and children, and when are we getting anywhere?" and things to that effect. They weren't violent or anything of that sort but they simply spoke up. They rebelled, as it were. And at that point in time, I crossed over and I heard Mr. Jankovic tell them that there was no need for panic, that they would remain there briefly, would be kept there till the end of the day, and then the buses would arrive and they would be taken and their families would arrive as well. You asked me what individuals these were. These were mostly Muslim men who had already been separated from the women and children at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did Colonel Jankovic tell them where they would be taken at that point? It's just not clear on the record, that's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As I mentioned a few moments ago, he said -- he told them that at the end of the day, buses would come to get them, and that their wives and children, their families, would arrive, and that really transpired. At the end of the day, the buses did come.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I guess what I'm getting at is did he say to them that they were going to be taken to Kladanj or they were going to be taken to some particular location at that point?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, the word "Kladanj" was repeatedly mentioned on that entire day. It was always said and it was mentioned to the women and the children and it referred to the men as well. Everyone, it was said, was being taken to Kladanj. It was mentioned on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that but did Colonel Jankovic say that at the particular time concerning the conversation that we are talking about now?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. It's been a long time. So I'm not sure whether he mentioned it then or not. I'm not sure. But he said what I've said earlier, that their families would arrive and that the buses would come and -- at the end of the day, but I can't recall anything else. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many men, if you can estimate, were in that yard near the house at the time that Colonel Jankovic said this, or at the time that they spoke up, as you say?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, if at the end of the day 10 to 15 buses left, and we said that there was some 70 people per bus, and this was already late in the afternoon, perhaps an hour or two before all the buses had gone, perhaps there were somewhat fewer of them than the number of people who had already gone, so let's say perhaps there were under 10 busloads at that point in time in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think we can probably work the math out. Did you see Colonel Jankovic relatively in the same area also on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what was he doing on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The same things he was doing on the 12th, except for that occasion when -- except that he didn't address those people there as he did the day before. He was standing around, walking up and down the road. He was jotting something down. And I assumed that maybe he didn't really trust me or the other police, the other military police, and I'm not sure, I can't really claim that, but I think he may have been counting the buses himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say you assume that he didn't really -- he might not have trusted you or the other police, can you tell us why you think that or why you would make that assumption?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I am saying this because I noticed that - I'm almost sure but I didn't look at the notes - I had the impression looking at him, following his movements, that he was also counting the vehicles. Why would he be counting them himself if we were already counting them? I mean, the conclusion is that he probably didn't trust us, believe us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Besides you and Mr. Ilic that you refer to, did you see Colonel Jankovic engaging any other police officers, military police, or other soldiers, or officers, while you were in Potocari, either on the 12th or the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can say with a lot of certainty that I did not see him address any police officers or the soldiers. A large number of soldiers were there. They were curious. They were there for various reasons. But I really have to say that they did kind of stop to exchange a few words with him. I don't know what they were talking about, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, we are running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see it is the break, and now is a good time to break, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to refer to page 57, lines 4 and 5, the numbers are not recorded properly. It should read P1095 and P1096. And if I recall correctly and understood the witness correctly, he wanted to make some remarks or corrections to the summary you read out at the beginning of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should consider that during the break. We adjourn and resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to pick up where Mr. President left off, and he indicated just before we broke, reminded me that you had some corrections, I think you wanted to make with respect to the summary that I read out a little bit earlier. Is that right, Mr. Janjic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't you tell us what you'd like to correct.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: First of all, at the beginning, at the very beginning of the summary, you mentioned two to three times "Janjic's group." This is incorrect, in my opinion. I think that it would be more realistic to say a group of military policemen including Mile Janjic, who was present, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. It was intended to mean the group that you were among, but I appreciate that. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: And at the end, a bus -- actually buses were mentioned in the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac. Persons arrived in the morning, you described them in black uniforms, and the buses departing. And then you say, when all the buses had left from the school and around school, Janjic went home, but I think that it should be that once the first buses left, I was in a specific area, and it was known where I was, so when those vehicles left that were in the immediate vicinity of the place where I was, I then left.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Janjic. If you could, and I think it might be helpful, just to remind us where you were when those vehicles left.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The whole time on the 13th, in the evening, when I was there, in the immediate vicinity of the Bratunac SUP, some 100 metres from the Vuk Karadzic school, closer to the SUP, where I was perhaps from the school to the SUP, it's 130 to 140 metres. This is the area where I was moving around. It's some 100 metres away from the school. There is a bakery nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. I'd like ask you a few other follow-up questions, if I may. First, I did mention this police officer named Ilic before. He was a civilian police officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did he wear a uniform similar to you? In other words, were civilian police uniforms similar to military police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The uniforms were not similar at all. We wore green camouflage uniforms. The police, the civilian police, wore blue camouflage uniforms. And on both those days that Mr. Ilic was in Potocari, he was in a blue police camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did the civilian police wear white belts, as you've indicated the military police did?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the white belts that the military police wore that you said, can you tell us, can you describe how those belts were worn?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The belts were worn so that they were visible. They were worn over the belt that you wore in your pants. They were worn over the waist belt. They were white. It wasn't a rule that all policemen had a pistol on their belt. We were issued only with automatic weapons. Only policemen who privately owned a pistol wore them. For example, I had a pistol that I owned, that was my own, and I wore it on my white belt, and there were a couple of colleagues, policemen, who wore pistols. They were not issued to us and it was not obligatory that we wear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you wear your belt across your shoulder, across your front? Did it cover that part of your body as well?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I know what you're asking. That kind of belt that was crossed across the chest, that is something that was worn in the -- I served in the regular JNA and I saw military police officers who wore that like that. None of us actually had that kind of belt. We wore a regular belt at the waist. Nobody wore these belts that were on the shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You certain of that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely sure, as far as the Bratunac Brigade military police is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned in your testimony that at a certain point, and you were not certain of the date, you went with some other MPs to Rocevic. Do you remember giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, it's a little unclear from your testimony, but can you tell us about how long a period you were there, you spent in Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I think that I always said that it was some 15 to 20 minutes, definitely not more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What was your assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't know what assignment it was at that time. I don't even know it now. I never knew it. I don't know why we went there, because we didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How long did it take for you to get there, from Bratunac is where I think you set out from?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We set out from Bratunac, we took a Pinzgauer and a combat vehicle. They were moving a bit more slowly. We needed more than an hour, maybe even an hour and a half, to reach that place. You don't need an hour if you're going by car, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. During the -- you said about 20 minutes that you were there, what specifically were you doing?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: When we arrived, and I said this a number of times, the vehicle stopped in front of a specific school at the back, in front of the gym, in the yard. A number of policemen didn't get out of the vehicle. I did. We got off there, we exchanged a few words with persons who were there already, we got into the vehicle again and returned towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think you indicated in your testimony that you were told at some point that there were prisoners in the school, or there were Muslims in the school. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I said earlier that we exchanged a few words with people who were already there. We made a few comments, we chatted, and I found out from them, and I will agree with you, that they had said that there were prisoners, Muslim prisoners, in the school, that they were in the school itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you P0094. And I have to go to page 191 in that exhibit. When you first arrived at the school, or in the area of the school, you mentioned that you saw some men from Zenica. They were part of the Bratunac Brigade. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Where did you see those men in relation to the school?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be easier, I already have the photo in front of me, I could show you, if possible. Or I could also say it, if I cannot point it out. As I'm looking at the photograph, there are two basketball baskets, one is in front, the other one is to the left, and then between those two hoops, looking towards the fence, there was a white personnel carrier of UNPROFOR. We are looking at an electricity pylon closer to the school. Before the right hoop is where the Pinz was parked, between the pole and the hoop. I came out, I was standing next to the APC, and these people were behind the left hoop as we are looking back towards the gym, on this area that is covered with asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I will have you mark this photograph. That would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Court Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do is to mark it with numbers and we'll describe what corresponds to the numbers, for the record. So can you tell us, can you mark with number 1 where you saw the men from Zenica, the soldiers you saw from Zenica, if you can see that on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you mark with number 2 where you saw the APC.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you mark with number 3 where you saw the Pinz, and that's the Pinzgauer, the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: When we came with the Pinzgauer. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you mark with number 4 where it was that you were, where you got out of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the other members -- were you the only member of your -- of the military police members that arrived at the school, were you the only one who got out of the vehicle, or were there others?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As I said earlier, only a few of us came out. Some people did not leave the vehicle. I said that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. That's sufficient for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to have this moved into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked photograph will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the marked portion of P0094 shall be given exhibit number P01446, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you page 190, in this exhibit. And I just want to clarify, for the record: Is this the school that you went to, that you've indicated in your prior testimony? I see that you've marked it and everything but I don't think I asked you if this was the school that you went to.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Neither one would be right. I didn't attend, nor did I enter it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I don't mean either, actually. I mean to ask you, the exhibit that you marked, does that show the school that you were -- where you were in Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It does look like that school, and I can say with certainty that that would be that school. I don't think that there is another one that would be similar, there is one that is exactly the same in Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see the school from this perspective now, what we can see on the screen? Did you see this side of the building while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The photograph where I made the markings, I had to have seen it when I was there. It's logical that I had seen it when I was already there. So I must have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'm referring to is the photograph that's now in the screen in front of you, which is different than the one that you marked. I don't know, maybe it hasn't changed in front of you, but did you have an opportunity to see the school from this perspective? You should see some grass and some trees on the screen in front of you. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I do have a photo on the screen. The picture is unclear. It's dark. The whole time I was talking about the picture that I marked. What I'm seeing here is quite dark. I really don't recognise it. I can't tell what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. We will try to adjust it for you so you can see it better.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about this photo because if it is the same school, this is taken from a side that I'm not familiar with. The view from the yard is something that I could be sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. That's why I asked the question. I appreciate your answer. Now, you mentioned in your testimony that you had the opportunity to see Mirko Jankovic at the school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The school in Bratunac is mentioned, the Vuk Karadzic school, and the school in Rocevic too. Which school are you thinking?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're right. I'm thinking of the school in Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I mentioned that I saw him in front of the school in Rocevic. You said earlier in the school, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in your testimony, you mentioned that he had a conversation with -- bear with me for a moment. He had a conversation with someone by the name of Zoran Zivanovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know if Zoran Zivanovic returned with the group of MPs that you arrived at Rocevic with? Did he return with you back to Bratunac or did he go -- did he remain at Rocevic or did he go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He really objected firmly with Mirko Jankovic. He protested. He said that there was no way he would stay, that he wanted to go back. I cannot state with certainty whether he returned with us or whether he sat with Mirko in the APC, the white APC. I really couldn't say which one it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony you indicated that you went back to Bratunac after leaving Rocevic. Do you know if other members of the Bratunac military police remained in the Zvornik area after that? And I say "Zvornik area" because I can -- I'm considering that Rocevic is in the Zvornik area, but generally that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I know for sure that all the military policemen, including myself, who came to Rocevic with the Pinz combat vehicle returned to Bratunac. I cannot say whether Zoran Zivanovic joined us, whether he came back with us or with Mirko. All the other policemen who went there returned together, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to show you P00018. These will be -- this is, I should say, the Bratunac military police daily logbook. Are you familiar with such a book?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I know that there was a duty logbook. I don't know if it's the same one that we are looking at now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you an entry in this book, and it's at page 19 of the B/C/S and it should be 16 in the English. It reads at the top, at least in the English, and you'll correct us if there is any error in the translation, it reads that it's a daily report, that the duty officer is Mile Petrovic, the deputy duty officer is Mladen Blagojevic, and then on duty at the bridge it reads Rajo Ilic and reception, M. Obackic. What I want to draw your attention to is the second sentence in this report, which reads, one patrol remained in Pilica to secure and guard the Muslims. All else went according to the plan of the military police command. What I'd like to know is, the reference here to the patrol remaining in Pilica to secure and guard the Muslims, can you tell us what that is about? Did you have any information about Bratunac military police in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have any information about that. I've never been to Pilica. I don't even know exactly where it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that you may not have been to Pilica but did you hear that other members of your unit, the Bratunac military police, were in Pilica on or about, as we can see here, what's dated as 17 July 1995? Either on that day or before that day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I've already answered: No, I didn't hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to show you page 22 in the B/C/S and what should be page 19 in the English. Here is another entry in this logbook, it indicates daily report, dated 20th July 1995, duty officer is S. Mijatovic. First, can you tell us who that is, if you know the first name?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: There was only one Mijatovic, that is Slobodan Mijatovic. He was one of the commanders. Deputy commander or a squad commander, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then we have deputy duty officer, Rajko Ilic. And then it says, "On duty at the bridge, Rade Micic," and in this particular report it indicates in the second sentence that two Muslims who were turned back from Serbia were also brought in and put in custody. What I'd like to know is, first, if you know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, and I would also mention the date, because what's a little bit odd in all of this is the fact that the majority of the policemen at that point in time were engaged in Potocari. I think we were there on that day. With the departure of the United Nations, our task was to secure, let's call it, the former base of the UN in Potocari, to prevent civilians from coming in and removing all the equipment and so on. It was a large compound and there was a large number of policemen who were on duty in Potocari for 24 hours a day. That's where I was the first few days. So maybe because of that. I don't know what was happening in the police building. We were spending two days up there, and after that we had one day off to go home. This is what our shifts were like. And this went on for more than 15 days, until all of the stuff was taken out from there. I don't know where it was taken. All of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could it be that the UNPROFOR base was vacated, shall we say, on the 21st of July 1995, not on the 20th? Could you be mistaken about that or are you certain? Maybe before you answer it, I should show you the following entry in this logbook. If we could go to, I guess it would be page 23 in the B/C/S, page 20 in the English. In the English, this particular entry says: "Patrols were engaged in securing the road for the passage of General Mladic. A patrol consisting of eight policemen was engaged in securing the UNPROFOR check-point at the battery factory." Does this refresh your recollection with respect to the entries in the notebook, or is this something totally different?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, it is plainly stated here, and that's the same thing that I mentioned earlier, that they were engaged in securing the UNPROFOR compound, and I didn't tell you the precise date. I just said that I think it would have been around those dates, it could have been the 19th or the 20th or the 21st.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The 11th, 12th, or the 13th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But here we can see that it's the 21st, actually, that was the first day, and why wouldn't I believe that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So let me return to my original question, which is about the two Muslims who were turned back from Serbia and put into custody. If we could go back to page 22 in the B/C/S and page 19 in the English so the witness has it in front of him. Have you heard anything about that? Let's start there.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, I really haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Where would these individuals have been put into custody, as is indicated here in the report?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: All individuals who were held in custody, I know where they were held, they were held at the police station building, and I know of two or three Muslims who were held in custody at the Bratunac Brigade command, but some escaped and that actually led to the removal of the entire squad of police, of military police, the ones before my -- before I became a member -- or that unit. And after their dismissal, a new, actually, military police unit was formed and I became a member of it, but as I said, I know that this happened before my time. I wasn't a member of the police at the time. There was a squad, and there was a room there with a grille on the windows, it was for conscripts that were brought in and held in custody, and if anyone was taken into custody, then they would have had to be brought there because that was the only room that could be used for it. The other rooms were the duty officer's room and there was one or two rooms -- there were one or two rooms for where the police officers slept during the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, on page 83, lines 5 through 10, there is some confusion about dates. Perhaps you could, for the sake of the record, clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I can't quite work out what that relates to, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me try and clarify something on the record. There appears to be something that may have not been recorded accurately. When I referred to the date that your unit secured the UNPROFOR compound, as was indicated in the logbook in an entry on 20 -- on the 21st of July, 1995, you had indicated that you were -- you hadn't given a precise date but were referring just generally to that period of time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. My answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we are now looking at the entry dated 20th July 1995, concerning these two Muslims that were turned back from Serbia and put in custody. You indicated that they would be taken to a police station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: You asked me where these persons, if they were taken into custody, could be brought. Now, whether that was actually the case, whether those two individuals were taken anywhere or not, I can't really say. But I described what the rooms look like that were used for -- as detention rooms, and I mentioned an instance with -- that had to do with the escape of some Muslims from some earlier period of time. I explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I appreciate that. Now, with respect to these particular individuals, I understand that you have no knowledge about their circumstances, as is indicated in this report. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I have no knowledge whatsoever, either whether they were brought in or whatever happened next.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. During the period of time that you were on duty in July 1995, were there other occasions where Muslim prisoners, people that had been captured, were put in the custody of the brigade? Of the military police unit in particular but of the brigade more generally?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were asked some questions in your previous testimony concerning Ljubisa Beara and somebody by the name of Pop. I want to ask you, as you sit here today, do you know who this individual by the name of Pop is, or was, I should say, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really know who Mr. Jankovic was referring to [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the translation, or the record reads a little oddly. It says that you don't know. "I really know who Mr. Jankovic was referring to." Do you mean you don't really know who Mr. Jankovic was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I said I really don't know who Mr. Jankovic was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks for clarifying that. Were you aware that the immediate superior unit to the brigade was the corps, in particular the Drina Corps, relative to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't go into that. I don't know. I know that I was a member of the Bratunac Brigade, the military police platoon. As for the rest, I really don't know anything about it. I know that the commander was Vidoje Blagojevic, and that's all -- that's the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Janjic. I have no further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are approaching 7.00. I don't know if it is a wise approach to commence your cross-examination. Perhaps it's better to start with that tomorrow, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to wish a good evening to this witness and just to say that we have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No questions at all in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, that's correct. We have no questions for this witness because the examination-in-chief was rather lengthy and in detail, so we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As there is no cross-examination, there will be no re-examination. Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination, your testimony, in this courtroom in this trial. Thank you very much for your attendance here and that you were able to help us and assist us finding the truth. You are now free to return to your normal activities, and the court officer will assist you. Thank you very much again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, and I would like to thank the Prosecutor and all the -- all those present as well as Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to adjourn for the day and resume tomorrow in the afternoon, 2.15 in this courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of December 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
